privacy.badge.title: Nothing leaves this computer. No account, no upload, no tracking.
home.title: Your scans, in 3D. Privately.
home.lead: Open the folder or ZIP you got from the hospital or diagnostic centre. medmereport builds an interactive 3D model and a full scan viewer — right here on your computer.
home.p1.d: Works offline. Nothing is uploaded, ever.
home.p2.d: Standard DICOM discs, encrypted discs (with your password), ZIPs, and X-ray images or PDFs.
home.p3.d: Learn what each part is and does. Your radiologist's report is the authority.
session.missing.d: For your privacy this page only works when opened by the medmereport app on this computer. Close this tab and start medmereport again.
disclaimer: For education only — not a diagnosis.
import.title: Open the scans from your hospital
import.mockNote: Demo mode: synthetic phantom data, no engine. Password for the locked disc is “phantom”.
import.choose.title: Where are your scans?
import.choose.lead: Insert the CD/DVD or USB from the hospital, or find the folder or ZIP you downloaded. Pick the top folder — we find the images inside.
import.paste.label: Paste a folder or file path
import.paste.hint: Tip: in Windows Explorer, Shift + right-click a folder → “Copy as path”.
import.browse.empty: No sub-folders or recognised files here. If this is the disc, choose “Open this folder”.
import.browse.error: This folder could not be opened. It may have been removed, or access is not allowed.
import.browse.noRoots: No drives found. Paste a path below instead.
import.found.title: Here’s what we found
import.remember: Remember this study on this computer
import.remember.hint: Off by default. If off, the processed images are wiped when medmereport closes. Nothing is ever uploaded.
import.privacy: Everything happens on this computer. Your scans are never uploaded.
import.pw.title: This disc is password protected
import.pw.lead: Enter the password to unlock the images.
import.pw.leadNamed: {label}: enter the password to unlock the images.
import.pw.where: It is usually printed on the slip, envelope or report that came with the disc from the hospital or diagnostic centre.
import.pw.label: Disc password
import.pw.wrong: That password didn’t unlock the disc. Check for mix-ups like 0/O or 1/l and capital letters.
import.pw.privacy: The password is used once to unlock the disc in memory. It is never saved, logged or sent anywhere.
import.progress.title: Opening your scans
import.progress.note: This usually takes under a minute. You can keep this tab open in the background.
import.err.no_images.d: We looked through this location but found no medical images (DICOM) or X-ray pictures.
import.err.no_images.next: Choose the top folder of the disc or the ZIP you received — the one that contains a DICOM or DICOMDIR folder.
import.err.unsupported.t: We don’t recognise this disc yet
import.err.unsupported.d: This disc or archive uses a format medmereport can’t read yet.
import.err.unsupported.next: Run “medmereport diagnose <path>” in a terminal. It makes a de-identified report (no names, no images) you can share so support can be added.
import.err.too_large.t: This is too large to open safely
import.err.too_large.d: The archive would expand beyond the safety limit. This protects your computer from damaged or malicious archives.
import.err.too_large.next: Extract the archive yourself and choose the extracted folder, or free up disk space and try again.
import.err.inspect_failed.t: We couldn’t look at that location
import.err.inspect_failed.d: The path may not exist, or medmereport isn’t allowed to read it.
import.err.inspect_failed.next: Check the path (copy it from your file manager) and that the disc is still inserted.
import.err.request_failed.d: The medmereport engine didn’t accept the request.
import.err.request_failed.next: Make sure medmereport is still running, then try again. Restarting it from its shortcut usually helps.
import.err.unknown.t: Something went wrong while opening the scans
import.err.unknown.next: Try again. If it keeps happening, run “medmereport diagnose <path>” and share the de-identified report.

seq.T1.name: T1-weighted
seq.T1.what: A T1-weighted image shows anatomy crisply: fat looks bright and fluid (like the fluid around the brain) looks dark.
seq.T1.why: Good for seeing the shape and structure of tissues. If contrast dye was given, areas that take it up look brighter.
seq.T2.name: T2-weighted
seq.T2.what: A T2-weighted image makes water and fluid look bright.
seq.T2.why: Helps show swelling, fluid and many tissue changes, which often look brighter than the normal tissue around them.
seq.FLAIR.name: FLAIR
seq.FLAIR.what: A T2-type image in which the signal from normal fluid (CSF) is switched off, so that fluid looks dark.
seq.FLAIR.why: Makes bright changes next to fluid spaces — such as around the ventricles — easier to see.
seq.DWI.name: Diffusion (DWI)
seq.DWI.what: Diffusion-weighted imaging measures how freely water molecules can move inside tissue.
seq.DWI.why: Areas where water movement is restricted look bright. Doctors read it together with the ADC map, for example when checking for a recent stroke.
seq.ADC.name: ADC map
seq.ADC.what: A map calculated from the diffusion images that shows how much water moves at each point.
seq.ADC.why: Read together with DWI: truly restricted areas look dark on ADC, which helps separate them from areas that only look bright on DWI.
seq.T2STAR.name: T2* (gradient echo)
seq.T2STAR.what: T2* images are very sensitive to tiny magnetic differences in tissue.
seq.T2STAR.why: Blood products, calcium and iron show up as dark spots, so it helps find small old bleeds.
seq.SWI.name: SWI
seq.SWI.what: Susceptibility-weighted imaging is an even more sensitive relative of T2*.
seq.SWI.why: Shows small veins, micro-bleeds and mineral deposits as dark lines or dots.
seq.TOF.name: Time-of-flight angiography
seq.TOF.what: TOF angiography makes flowing blood bright without any injected dye.
seq.TOF.why: Used to look at the arteries of the head and neck, such as the ring of arteries at the base of the brain (Circle of Willis).
seq.STIR.name: STIR
seq.STIR.what: A fluid-sensitive image in which the signal from fat is suppressed.
seq.STIR.why: Makes swelling in bone, muscle and soft tissue stand out; common in spine scans.
seq.PD.name: Proton density
seq.PD.what: Proton-density images reflect how much water (hydrogen) each tissue contains.
seq.PD.why: Shows fine detail of cartilage, ligaments and menisci; often used for joints.
seq.CT.name: CT
seq.CT.what: Computed tomography combines X-rays taken from many angles into thin slices. Bone is bright and air is black.
seq.CT.why: Fast and very good for bone, bleeding, lungs and many emergencies.
seq.CTA.name: CT angiography
seq.CTA.what: A CT scan taken while contrast dye flows through the blood vessels.
seq.CTA.why: Shows the shape of arteries, and any narrowing or bulging, in fine detail.
seq.CR.name: X-ray (CR)
seq.CR.what: A classic X-ray picture captured on a reusable imaging plate.
seq.CR.why: A quick overview picture of bones, chest or joints. It is a single projection, so structures overlap.
seq.DX.name: Digital X-ray
seq.DX.what: A single X-ray picture captured directly by a digital detector.
seq.DX.why: Quick overview images, for example of the chest, spine or a joint.
seq.MIP.name: Maximum-intensity projection
seq.MIP.what: The brightest points through the whole stack, squeezed into one picture — often shown rotating around.
seq.MIP.why: Gives a 3D-like view of bright structures, such as the blood vessels on an angiogram.
seq.PHOTO.name: Photo or scanned page
seq.PHOTO.what: A photograph or scanned page (for example of a film or report), not a measured scan.
seq.PHOTO.why: Useful for viewing, but it has no physical scale, so measurements are not possible.
viewer.tool.scroll.hint: Drag up/down to move through slices — or use the mouse wheel
viewer.tool.wl.hint: Drag to change brightness/contrast (window/level) — or right-drag
viewer.tool.pan.hint: Drag to move the image — or middle-drag
viewer.tool.zoom.hint: Drag to zoom — or Ctrl + wheel to zoom at the cursor
viewer.tool.measure.hint: Drag to measure a distance in millimetres
viewer.reset.hint: Reset zoom, contrast and measurements (or double-click the image)
viewer.labels.hint: Colour the computer-estimated regions and name them on hover
viewer.link.hint: Link scrolling: parallel panes follow the same physical position
viewer.noMeasure: Measuring isn’t possible here: this image (a photo or scanned page) has no physical scale.
viewer.loadFailed: These images could not be loaded.
viewer.localizer.aria: The line on {ref} shows where the current slice is
view.title: All scans
view.disclaimer: This viewer is for personal education. It is not a diagnostic tool, and any region labels are computer estimates. Your radiologist’s report is the authoritative reading of these images.
view.hover.d: Turn on “Regions” and move over the image to name structures.
view.sagittal.title: Side view (sagittal)
view.sagittal.intro: Each slice is a side-on cut through the body, front of the body on the left. Scroll towards the middle slices to see the midline — the brainstem and spinal cord running down the spinal canal, with the vertebrae in front.
view.noSagittal: No side-view (sagittal) series in this study
view.noSagittal.d: Open the full scan viewer from the study page to see the other series.
help.touch: Zoom on touch screens; one finger scrolls
